I've hit my head on walls and floors ever since I was young. I sometimes still do it but I don't exactly know why. I have anxiety and a rough childhood. I want to change my behavior, but I don't know how to stop or even why I'm doing it.

The best way to handle anxiety of this level is through a combination of appropriate medical guidance and therapy. Engaging in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) can help you understand the thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that contribute to your anxiety. It's crucial to work with a therapist trained in trauma-informed therapy, especially given your history. They will help you recognize the reasons behind hitting your head and assist you in developing healthier coping mechanisms. It's great that you're aware of the issue and are seeking to address it. Wishing you the best on your healing journey!
Provide support and understanding to individuals experiencing emotional and psychological challenges. Focus on conversation style, insights and therapy.

I had a female friend who I decided to stop talking to because I found her behavior concerning. When she would call, I wouldn't answer, which made my girlfriend suspicious. She keeps asking me why I don't answer that call, and I told her I don't want to be friends with this woman. However, I don’t think my girlfriend believes me. How can I help her understand my decision?

It's understandable that your girlfriend is feeling suspicious, especially in a culture that often promotes the idea that evasiveness signals something deeper. To help her feel more secure, consider being transparent about your relationship with this woman. Explain how you met, the duration of your friendship, and your reasons for ending it—clarifying what you mean by 'concerning behavior.' It may also help to reassure her of your commitment by highlighting what makes your relationship special. You could express that, out of all the women you could be with, you chose her and would do so again. Engaging in thoughtful gestures that show your affection might also help reinforce her trust in you. Ultimately, fostering open dialogue can strengthen your relationship. Best of luck!
Provide support and understanding to individuals experiencing emotional and psychological challenges. Focus on conversation style, insights and therapy.

My long-distance girlfriend is in a sorority, and it's changing her. I feel like I'm becoming less important to her and it hurts. She wants my support for the sorority, but it's challenging for me. I try every day to show her she's the most important thing to me, but she struggles to stay sober at parties, which worries me. We love each other, but we're going through a tough time.

You may already be doing a lot for your relationship. Remember, each of you contributes equally to it. It's essential to discuss whether your understanding of the current issues in your relationship aligns with hers. A helpful conversation might involve defining the problem together as a couple. This can ensure that you both have similar values and expectations regarding your partnership. Since these discussions can evoke strong emotions, it might be beneficial to revisit them multiple times. Consider seeking help from a licensed therapist who can assist both of you in exploring your emotional connections in a supportive environment. Best of luck in understanding and appreciating your relationship!

Cheating is something unacceptable for me, but because we have two daughters, I decided not to break up the family. However, now I am struggling to forget and forgive what happened. I feel like I cannot trust him. Without trust, I cannot stay in this relationship. On the other hand, I do not want my children to get hurt. I'm not sure how to move forward.

It is completely understandable that you are struggling to forgive and forget this betrayal. Infidelity takes time to heal from, so allow yourself to grieve and find the support you need. I suggest considering couples therapy and addressing whether there has been genuine remorse, transparency, and responsibility taken for the infidelity, as this has a significant impact on trust and your relationship. If there are doubts about trust, he needs to be willing to earn it back and actively work on the relationship. It's important to acknowledge and accept your feelings of hurt and pain, as they will likely come in waves, but with time and supportive therapy, the pain can lessen. Keep in mind that parents model healthy relationship behavior for their children, so whether you heal together or separately, it is crucial for your children's emotional and psychological development to see healthy communication and boundaries in relationships. Take care of yourself, and I wish you much peace and healing.
Provide support and understanding to individuals experiencing emotional and psychological challenges. Focus on conversation style, insights and therapy.

I have twin toddlers. I experienced the death of a loved one before giving birth, and I had a difficult breakup with the father. People have suggested he was using me for financial reasons. My ex-boyfriend had extreme meltdowns recently, and I often feel alone with no friends.

First, it’s important to acknowledge your strength in managing such significant challenges. Caring for twins on your own is indeed a demanding situation. Anxiety can arise when we have so much on our plates. There are various strategies to manage and lessen symptoms of anxiety, and it’s crucial to find what resonates with you personally. Connecting with friends, a counselor, or trusted individuals can provide valuable support as you explore different approaches. Remember to take a moment for yourself: find a safe space, take a deep breath in, and slowly exhale, asking yourself what you need in that moment so you can move forward.

My fiancé and I broke up. He cheated on me numerous times. I kept forgiving him but was constantly questioning his actions. Eventually, he got tired and left.

Cheating reflects a lack of commitment and leads to significant emotional pain. It seems that while you may have attempted to forgive him, your continuous questioning suggests unresolved feelings. True forgiveness often requires understanding and empathy from the person who caused the hurt. From what you've shared, it appears your fiancé did not take steps to rebuild your trust or recognize the impact of his actions on you. His departure might also symbolize a shared exhaustion with the dynamics of your relationship. Although it may be difficult to cope with this disappointment, it seems that the situation was unsatisfying for both of you.

My wife recently said she wants a divorce, and it feels sudden. I understand that marriages have ups and downs, but I don't know why she won't explain her reasons. Should I fight for my family, which includes my daughter and wife?

It's possible that there were earlier signs of issues in your marriage, which may have seemed like typical ups and downs. It’s important to understand your wife’s perspective to identify if the issues can be addressed. I encourage you to talk to her about working on the marriage and consider seeing a marriage counselor together. Be open to her feedback and try not to react defensively. Remember, a divorce doesn't mean you will no longer be a part of your daughter's life. It's important to maintain your involvement in her life. If divorce does occur, aim to handle the situation as amicably as possible to minimize any negative impact on your daughter.

A good therapist will discuss what brought you to therapy in the first place and co-create a therapy plan that addresses the issues you want to work on. This plan is flexible, allowing for adjustments based on what arises during sessions. Additionally, you will agree on the frequency and scheduling of your meetings.

Often, it's not just about forgiveness but about learning from our experiences. For example, when we learn to walk as children, we fall repeatedly but through that process, we learn to take steady steps. These experiences help us grow and understand the consequences of our actions. Over time, as you reflect on what happened, forgiveness may come as part of your journey towards moving forward.

My last relationships have ended horribly. They just up and abandoned me. One of them I have never gotten closure with over it, leaving me emotionally wrecked. I know something's wrong with me but I don't know how to even start trying to better myself. I get into these depressed-like states whenever anyone I care about is too busy to be with me. I know that I shouldn't act like that because people are genuinely busy, but I feel like they're doing it just because they don't want to be around me.

Frequently when working with clients, I utilize the A-B-C model developed by the founder of Rational Emotive Behavior Theory. The theory states that you cannot control an event but you can control your reaction to the emotions associated with that event. For instance, here's an example: A (Action or Event): You need to talk to someone and that person is not calling you back. B (Behavior or Response): You might tell yourself that this person is too busy for you or that you are not important to them. C (Consequence): You feel depressed. If you look at the model, B has a direct effect on C. The thought is that if you change your reaction to A, then C could have a better outcome. For example: A stays the same. B (this is what you change): This person must be busy; they will call me back when they get a chance, or I can call someone else for support until this person is available. C: Decreased feelings of depression and improved overall functioning. Actively working to replace negative thought patterns can lead to improvements in your overall outlook and mood. If this model resonates with you, seeking support groups in your area can also be a great source of support when you are feeling abandoned or alone.

I keep having these random thoughts that I don't want. Thoughts like 'you aren't worth anything.' They feel like they come from someone else. What is wrong with me, and how can I stop having these thoughts?

Many people experience unwelcome or negative thoughts occasionally. Learning to manage these thoughts and reframing your self-perception is often a key focus in counseling. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is an effective approach that can help you address these feelings and develop healthier thought patterns.

I have been feeling more and more down recently. I have started having trouble sleeping due to panic attacks, but they are almost never triggered by something that I know of.

Answers about our inner lives are most successfully reached from a sense of feeling grounded in oneself. The first step is to accept your nervousness and restless sleep. As often as possible, try to sleep during random times in order for your body to catch up on its need for rest. It's also important to accept feeling down, as it's normal to feel that way once in a while. From this place of self-acceptance, trust any answers that come to your mind. Often, answers about complicated topics come in small pieces, not all at once. Regarding panic attacks, they are also quite normal and often arise without a clear trigger. They are a healthy symptom your body uses to manage difficult emotions. Therefore, self-acceptance, tolerance for the process of emotional clearing, and embracing your sleep patterns are ways to help stabilize yourself, which will ultimately feel calming and beneficial.

I'm starting therapy soon and I'm really nervous. My main fear is that I'll cry and embarrass myself. Should I be worried about that?

Many people cry during their therapy sessions, and it's quite common. It's important to know that it's safe to express your emotions in this environment. Crying is a normal human response to pain and is not a sign of weakness. In fact, trying to suppress those emotions can often lead to more harm. Allowing yourself to cry can be a cleansing experience and an important part of the healing process.

My boyfriend has a close female friend, and it bothers me because of their closeness. I decided to meet her, but it only made things worse because they acted more like a couple than friends. Although there was no physical interaction, he talks to her a lot. What can I do? Leaving him isn't an option.

It's understandable to feel hurt by your boyfriend's closeness with his female friend. It's good that you were able to observe their dynamic. Unfortunately, you cannot control his relationship with her, but you can express your discomfort directly to him. Sharing your feelings may prompt him to reconsider how he interacts with her. It's important to acknowledge that the control ultimately lies with him. Since leaving the relationship isn't an option for you, it might be helpful to come to terms with this aspect of his life. If after trying to address your feelings and adjusting to the situation you still feel dissatisfied, it may be worth considering a long-term plan to reevaluate your relationship in the future.

I'm very depressed. How do I find someone to talk to?

I'm sorry to hear that you're feeling this way. It's important to reach out for support. You might consider calling a local helpline or talking to a family doctor who can help you find a therapist. I hope you find someone to talk to soon.

How do I decide if I should end my relationship with my boyfriend?

This can be a very challenging decision, and it may take time for you to sort through all of your feelings about the relationship and its possible end. Therapy can provide a space for you to be completely honest with yourself about your relationship as you navigate your decision on whether to remain with your boyfriend. A therapist can ask questions to help you uncover your true feelings about whether this is the right relationship for you and can support you in whatever decision you come to.

I am going through a very hard time and I'm so depressed. My parents are getting a divorce and a lot of bad things are happening.

It sounds like a tough time and it's normal to feel down when your family is going through a divorce or other hardship. There's a difference between feelings like sadness, discouragement, grief, loneliness, and depression, though. Sadness is a natural reaction to events in our lives, while depression often feels like being stuck. Engaging in self-care can be a healthy way to support yourself during this difficult time. It's important to name your feelings and share them with someone you trust; this can bring comfort. For the aspects of what you're experiencing that relate to depression—such as feeling stuck, trouble concentrating, changes in sleep and appetite, loss of enjoyment in activities, poor hygiene, and feelings of hopelessness—it's important to identify these symptoms. If you have any thoughts of hurting yourself, please talk to someone. Consider calling a support line for guidance. First aid for depression includes daily self-care, maintaining good sleeping and eating habits, regular exercise—even when it feels challenging—and fostering positive self-talk. If you find it difficult to lift yourself out of depression, seeking help from a professional can be beneficial. They can assist with setting short-term goals and offer support. It may also be worth discussing with a healthcare provider about the possibility of short-term medication to help during this rough patch. Best wishes.

If you don't feel comfortable discussing sensitive topics with them, it's okay to give yourself permission to step back from those conversations. Focus on what feels safe and supportive for you.

Has your former partner made any efforts to be in contact with you in order to restart your relationship? From what you describe, your former partner is in a new relationship. It is possible that since you love her and would like to be together again, that you are misinterpreting her actions. If you'd like to have more certainty as to whether she is cheating or if she is happy in her new relationship, you could consider reaching out to her and asking directly. However, a healthier path may be to acknowledge your sadness about her being with someone else. It's important to respect your feelings and recognize that the relationship didn't unfold as you had hoped.

It sounds like you have been through a lot of pain, and dealing with grief can be incredibly challenging. The loss of a family member often brings up complicated feelings and can affect relationships within the family. It's important to seek support for your sadness, and setting boundaries with your sister might help you heal at your own pace. Finding someone to talk to about these feelings could also be beneficial.

I am becoming a Water Safety Instructor but I didn't have enough for a proper swimsuit. I was told by someone in class that my top was displaying everything. I was very embarrassed.

It's common to feel worse due to our own thoughts about situations we can't change. Overcoming embarrassment and self-blame can be challenging. By tuning into your internal dialogue, you might notice that your feelings are linked to your thoughts. Often, when we hold onto embarrassment, we might think things like, 'How could I do that?' or 'Now people saw things I didn't want them to see!' These self-sabotaging thoughts can lead to shame and embarrassment. Instead, try to identify more rational thoughts, such as, 'We all make mistakes,' or 'This incident does not define me.' Remember, people have diverse perceptions, and not everyone will see things the same way. By practicing these rational thoughts regularly, you can start to feel better and your embarrassment will diminish.

I am always arguing with my father. He gets stressed over work and health and talks to me in a tone that feels demanding and more like yelling. I often get upset by this. Am I too sensitive? He says I am overreacting but doesn't seem to understand that he is hurting my feelings. No matter how often I try to tell him, he never listens.

Thank you for sharing your concerns. It's important to recognize that wanting better communication with your father is valid, regardless of how sensitive you feel. When we feel talked down to or ridiculed, it can be hard not to take it personally. You’ve taken a valuable step by bringing this issue up to him. Consider whether your approach may lead him to feel blamed or defensive. It could be helpful to talk during a calm moment rather than in the heat of the moment. Use 'I' statements, like 'I feel upset when the tone is raised,' instead of accusatory language. Avoid absolute phrases like 'never' or 'always'. Suggest ways he might communicate more effectively since he might not realize how his tone affects you. Lastly, consider starting the conversation with something positive and ending it with another positive, using something like: 'Dad, I appreciate our discussions and value your opinion. Sometimes I feel hurt when I perceive harshness in your tone. Perhaps we could work on communicating more calmly during sensitive topics together.' I hope this advice helps you navigate the situation!
Provide support and understanding to individuals experiencing emotional and psychological challenges. Focus on conversation style, insights and therapy.

I crossdress and enjoy expressing my feminine side, but I find that my attraction to women causes some discomfort for the girls I date or ask out. How should I approach this subject with them? Should I keep it a secret or be upfront about it? I'm also conflicted about whether I should continue crossdressing since it makes me happy.

Thank you for sharing your thoughts. It's clear that your happiness is a priority, and I encourage you to continue doing what makes you feel joyful. Regarding how to disclose your crossdressing to potential partners, it may not be necessary to address it right away. Consider the timing based on your relationship and the person you’re dating. If you're pursuing a long-term relationship, honesty about significant aspects of yourself is important. Remember, if someone is uncomfortable with your crossdressing, it doesn't reflect anything wrong with you; it may simply be their personal preference. Think about the expectations of the people you are talking to and whether they might have questions. Are you prepared to discuss what crossdressing means to you and why it's important? Perhaps you can approach the conversation by inviting open dialogue and encouraging questions before they form judgments. I understand this might be a stressful situation, especially if you've experienced negative reactions in the past. Speaking with a therapist could offer you valuable support as you navigate these conversations.

He isn't violent, but he has anger issues and deep insecurities. He’s working on them and has improved. We started counseling, and he participated in one or two individual sessions, but we broke up again shortly thereafter. Now his constant questions and accusations are getting really draining.

Sometimes relationships just do not work out. It's important to understand that the first few relationships may not be the ones that last a lifetime. The right relationship will require effort but shouldn't be constantly draining or filled with turmoil. It's commendable that you both attended counseling, although one or two sessions might not be sufficient to effect change. It takes time and mutual effort to work towards a collective goal. It might be beneficial for you to focus on your own personal growth now. If he truly wants to develop alongside you, he will take the necessary steps. If not, it’s okay to wish him well and move forward.
Provide support and understanding to individuals experiencing emotional and psychological challenges. Focus on conversation style, insights and therapy.

I am in a complicated situation with my ex-fiancé, whom I am still seeing. He left me due to pressure from his teenage daughters who want him to reconcile with their mother. Although we separated not long ago, we have been seeing each other regularly, despite him living with his ex and children. His daughters are against our relationship due to my adult sons' past issues, which they find embarrassing. He wants me to wait as he tries to mend his relationship with them, even though we had planned to marry soon and everything was set up.

It sounds like you're in a very challenging situation. It's important to consider whether this relationship is healthy for you. Are you finding joy in the uncertainty, or is it causing you distress? It's okay to reflect on the benefits of remaining in this connection. Ask yourself if this relationship aligns with your well-being and happiness. Sometimes, waiting for someone to come around can adversely affect your self-esteem. Recognizing when to wait and when to move on is crucial, and only you can make that determination. Trust your instincts, and if it helps, seeking guidance from a counselor may provide clarity on any deeper issues you want to explore.

My girlfriend just quit drinking and she became really depressed. She told me that she wants to move. What can I do to help her? I want her to stay.

You should start by speaking with her about what has her feeling down. Have there been some significant events in her life that have affected her? Are there any challenges in your relationship that could be impacting both of you? Since she has recently stopped drinking, she may be struggling to find alternative and healthier behaviors. This is something you can explore together. Additionally, if needed, she might find it helpful to speak with a therapist to discuss her feelings about quitting alcohol. It sounds like you care deeply, and she could benefit from your support, even if she seems to be pushing you away.

I am in my early 20s and still live with my parents because I can't afford to live alone. My mother says that if I live under her roof, I have to follow her rules. She is trying to control my life. What should I do?

You're not alone; many young adults live with their parents for financial reasons. Are the rules your mother is referring to related to household organization or something more personal? Every household needs to have guidelines to maintain order, like cleanliness and shared responsibilities. Have you considered discussing your willingness to be a responsible member of the household while also expressing your desire for privacy in other areas of your life? This approach could help establish a respectful dialogue about boundaries.

I often find myself thinking scary thoughts, and sometimes I scare myself into believing something bad is going to happen. Once these thoughts start, they continue to loop in my mind, and I can't seem to stop them. How can I manage these thoughts?

Hello! It's essential to recognize that having such thoughts is quite common. Research indicates that a significant majority of human thoughts can be negative, so you're certainly not alone in this experience. I like to compare troubling thoughts to a tornado: when you're caught up in one, it can be overwhelming and makes it hard to focus on anything else. However, if you can step back and observe it from a distance, you gain perspective and can still take action to prioritize what matters to you. Here are three steps you can consider to create that distance: 

1. Label your thoughts by saying, 'I am noticing I am having the thought that...' For example, 'I am noticing I am having the thought that something bad is going to happen.' This doesn't aim to eliminate the thought but allows you to acknowledge it without getting swept up in it. 

2. Tune into your body and the sensations that arise. Notice where you feel tension or discomfort. Breathe into those areas and allow space for those feelings. Emotions such as joy, sadness, anxiety, shame, and anger are all part of being human. Recognizing them without resistance can help reduce their intensity. 

3. Stay grounded in the present moment. You can do this by engaging your five senses: what do you hear, see, taste, smell, and feel? Observing your body's responses, such as your breathing rate or temperature, can also anchor you in the here and now. 

Remember, while it's impossible to completely eliminate thoughts and feelings, the goal is to accept them while focusing on what is meaningful in your life. I hope these suggestions are helpful for you!
Provide support and understanding to individuals experiencing emotional and psychological challenges. Focus on conversation style, insights and therapy.
I'm always listening to my husband, but it feels like he never listens to me. How do I get him to listen to me instead of me always listening to him?

Have you two ever talked about how you feel? It might be a good start, as addressing the issue directly can help improve your communication. You could say something like, 'I'm feeling unhappy in our relationship because I don't feel heard.' This approach can open the door for a more constructive conversation. Let him know that you value being a good listener, but it's important for you to feel listened to as well. If he interrupts, it's okay to politely ask him to let you finish. Highlighting the importance of communication in a relationship is crucial. If he seems resistant to change, consider suggesting couples counseling as a way to navigate these issues together.

I'm a guy. If I don't like girls, nor do I like guys, does that mean I'm gay?

Hi, and thanks for your question. It's great to hear that you're exploring your feelings. I want to add a couple of things about asexuality: There are many misconceptions surrounding it. Some people who identify as asexual may have varying degrees of interest in sex. It's also important to understand that sexual orientations can be more diverse than just straight, gay, lesbian, or bisexual. Keep exploring your feelings; there's likely a community of people who share similar experiences. Remember, while labels can help some, it's crucial to take your time and not feel pressured to label yourself too quickly. This is your unique journey, and it's perfectly fine if you choose not to label how you feel. Hope this helps. Be well.
Provide support and understanding to individuals experiencing emotional and psychological challenges. Focus on conversation style, insights and therapy.

I've never been able to talk with my parents. They do not take me seriously when I talk about serious events in my life. If my dad doesn’t believe me, then my mom goes along with him and acts like she doesn’t believe me either. I'm a pansexual, but I can’t trust my own parents. I've fought depression and won; however, stress and anxiety are overwhelming me. I feel like my friends don't listen to me. I know they have their own problems, which I try to help with, but they don't always support me when I need it. I feel as if I've lost my childhood and that I have no one to trust.

One of the most challenging experiences is feeling unheard, especially by those close to us like parents. It's understandable to feel frustrated and hurt when they don't seem to listen. Sometimes, older generations may struggle to understand the unique challenges younger people face. I encourage you to have an open discussion with your parents about how you feel, perhaps at a time when emotions aren't running high. Let them know in advance that you have something important to share. Using 'I' statements can be helpful; for example, express how their actions affect you rather than placing blame. Also, sharing what you wish to see change can guide them towards understanding your perspective. If you're feeling overwhelmed, consider seeking support from a therapist or a school counselor who can provide a safe space to explore your feelings further. Best of luck to you.
Provide support and understanding to individuals experiencing emotional and psychological challenges. Focus on conversation style, insights and therapy.
I've been called names by others, and I'm fed up with it. I can't handle it anymore and feel awful. I've talked to someone about it, which is why I'm reaching out now.

It sounds like you are feeling overwhelmed by these experiences and the criticism from others. It's commendable that you are reaching out, and it shows your desire for change. Working with a qualified therapist could be a beneficial step to gain clarity, develop coping strategies, and ultimately find relief from these distressing feelings.

He's been losing feelings and he doesn't know why. I love him very much. He sometimes thinks I'm obsessed when I'm not at all. I give him his space and I make sure he's okay, but I think if we saw each other more, it would be better. It's hard not to stress about it because the love of my life is losing feelings, which is sad. He's a great guy, and I don't know why he's been losing feelings towards me. He's starting to put less effort into talking to me. I'll do anything to make us better as a couple. I've tried talking to him, but he doesn't like discussing it much. What should I do?

It sounds like a difficult situation. One approach could be to give him some space for now. It can be challenging, but sometimes when we press too hard to talk about issues, it can push our partner further away. It’s important for both of you to feel whole as individuals in a relationship. I also wonder how you find ways to soothe and calm yourself outside of this relationship. Focusing on your well-being during this time could be beneficial.

I want us all to get along, but I feel that I am not being respected. I have some insecurities because my boyfriend was with his ex for a while. He wants to see his stepdaughter, but his ex makes it difficult for me to be around. Although she has a boyfriend, my boyfriend goes over to see his ex and their child regularly. Since he works nights, I only see him part of the week, and he won't let me use his phone because of past issues with his ex. I don't think he's cheating, but he does lie about the time he leaves her place or when he goes over there. I feel like the other woman sometimes. His ex has also tried to interfere with holiday plans. Despite this, I think he is a wonderful boyfriend, but I'm concerned about how attached he still is to his past.

How much have you communicated your feelings about your boyfriend's relationship with his ex to him? The issues you’re experiencing are central to any intimate relationship. The positive aspect here is your awareness of your needs and expectations from a partner. It's important to address these feelings directly, as discussing them could lead to deeper emotions. If things get too overwhelming, consider seeking help from a couples' therapist who can facilitate these conversations and keep them focused, ensuring both perspectives are addressed.
Provide support and understanding to individuals experiencing emotional and psychological challenges. Focus on conversation style, insights and therapy.

I'm a Christian teenage girl who has lost my virginity. My boyfriend is also a Christian teenager, and things got out of hand sexually. I had planned to abstain from sex, but I wasn't clear about this because I was tempted and led him on. Now, I'm questioning if this means he isn’t the one God intended for me. We are young, yet I dream of a potential future together. I believe he is in my life for an important reason, and I am grateful I escaped from several abusive relationships because of him. I love him very much.

I may not have a strong religious perspective, but it seems that if you love him and want to be with him, then something like this shouldn't determine if he is the one for you. Sex can be viewed as an expression of love and commitment. If you see a future with him and want to marry him, it's worth considering why you feel the need to wait until marriage. Often, people believe depression is primarily about feeling 'sad,' but it can manifest through irritability, as you've mentioned, and a lack of energy. According to the DSM-V (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders), common symptoms of depression include: - Depressed mood - Irritable mood - Decreased interest or pleasure in previously enjoyed activities - Significant weight change or change in appetite - Changes in sleep patterns (insomnia or hypersomnia) - Psychomotor agitation or retardation - Fatigue or loss of energy - Feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt - Diminished ability to concentrate or indecisiveness - Thoughts of suicide or plans. The good news is that there are many ways to improve depressive symptoms. A beneficial first step is to consider seeing a physician or therapist who can help assess the severity of the depression and suggest methods for addressing it that align with your lifestyle and values.
